strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously flagged open problem: extending generalization guarantees for data-driven hyperparameter tuning from the one-dimensional case (Balcan et al. 2025) to the practically important multi-dimensional hyperparameter setting.

The core technical idea—casting the indicator of the bi-level loss exceeding a threshold as a polynomial first-order formula and using quantifier elimination together with the Goldberg-Jerrum (GJ) framework—is a clean and general mechanism that unifies training-loss and validation-loss settings under one theorem (Theorem 4.1).

The framework removes restrictive regularity assumptions (e.g., ELICQ conditions) required by the prior geometric approach, and also extends beyond piecewise-polynomial structure to general semi-algebraic functions, enabling new applications (weighted group LASSO, which is not piecewise polynomial).

The paper improves on the existing Goldberg & Jerrum (1993) bound for polynomial FOL pseudo-dimension by removing dependence on data dimension q and an extra factor of p, which is a concrete quantitative advance.

Section 7 provides a refined analysis exploiting explicit solution paths that yields tighter bounds and is shown to recover a tight (matching lower bound) sample complexity rate for a known problem (data-driven ElasticNet tuning, matching Balcan et al. 2023), which is a valuable sanity check on the tightness of the general machinery.
The applications in Section 8 (weighted group lasso, weighted fused lasso) concretely instantiate the abstract framework and demonstrate versatility beyond the piecewise-polynomial assumption class.
weaknesses: The work is entirely theoretical with no empirical validation; there are no experiments to illustrate that the derived pseudo-dimension bounds are meaningful/non-vacuous in realistic regimes, or to sanity-check the practical implications of the framework (e.g., comparing predicted sample complexity to empirically observed generalization gaps).

The general bounds in Theorems 5.1/6.1 scale multiplicatively/polynomially in p, d (and for Theorem 4.1 with products over quantifier blocks), and it is unclear from the paper how tight these general bounds actually are outside the special refined cases of Section 7; the paper only demonstrates tightness for the narrower explicit-solution-path setting (ElasticNet), leaving the tightness of the main, more general results largely unaddressed.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior building blocks: the paper largely combines existing tools (Basu et al.'s quantifier elimination complexity bounds, Bartlett et al.'s GJ framework, Balcan et al.'s data-driven algorithm design formulation) rather than introducing fundamentally new proof techniques; the contribution is more a careful, well-executed synthesis and generalization than a conceptual breakthrough.

The paper does not discuss computational tractability of actually solving the empirical risk minimization (ERM) problem over multi-dimensional hyperparameters in this bi-level setting, which is an important complementary concern to statistical learnability for practical adoption.

The presentation is dense, with most proofs deferred to a long appendix, and the paper would benefit from more intuition/exposition connecting the abstract FOL-based bounds to concrete numbers or realistic hyperparameter tuning scenarios (e.g., typical values of p, d and what sample sizes the bounds imply).

Fundamental lower bounds for the general bi-level (validation) setting remain open, which the authors acknowledge, but this leaves a gap between the (possibly loose) general upper bounds and the true statistical complexity of the harder validation-tuning problem that motivates much of the paper.

strengths: Addresses a concretely stated open problem (generalizing Balcan et al. 2025's one-dimensional, single-level hyperparameter generalization guarantees to the multi-dimensional, bi-level setting), which is a reasonable and well-motivated theoretical gap.

The core technical device—casting the indicator of the loss class as a polynomial first-order logic (FOL) formula and invoking quantifier elimination (Basu et al.) combined with the Goldberg-Jerrum pseudo-dimension machinery—is a clean, general-purpose reduction that cleanly separates the 'logical definability' question from the 'statistical complexity' question, and plausibly removes the ad hoc geometric/regularity assumptions (e.g., ELICQ conditions) required by the prior work.

The paper shows the generality of the framework by handling cases beyond the piecewise-polynomial assumption of prior work (e.g., weighted group LASSO, whose regularizer is semi-algebraic but not piecewise polynomial), and by deriving refined, solution-path-based bounds (Section 7) that in at least one worked example (ElasticNet) provably match a known lower bound from Balcan et al. (2023), which is a nice sanity check on tightness.

The paper is organized in a logical progression (general FOL tool → training-loss application → validation-loss application → refined bounds via solution paths → concrete applications), and the comparison against the only directly comparable prior general bound (Goldberg & Jerrum, 1993) is explicit and shows a quantifiable improvement (removal of dependence on instance dimension q and an extra factor of p).
weaknesses: The paper is entirely theoretical with zero empirical validation: there is no experiment, simulation, or numerical illustration showing that the derived bounds are non-vacuous, meaningfully tighter than naive discretization-based guarantees, or informative in any realistic regime of p, d, M, Δ. Given the stated motivation ('practically important' multi-dimensional tuning), the complete absence of any empirical grounding is a significant gap.

Except for the narrow special cases treated via the refined solution-path analysis (Section 7, e.g., ElasticNet and weighted fused LASSO), none of the main bounds (Theorems 4.1, 5.1, 6.1, 8.1) are shown or argued to be tight; it is unclear whether the general FOL/quantifier-elimination route produces bounds that are close to optimal or substantially loose, which undercuts the claim of 'sharper, more broadly applicable guarantees.'

The paper provides no discussion of computational tractability for actually finding the empirical risk minimizer α̂ in the multi-dimensional, non-convex, bi-level setting. Quantifier elimination algorithms (Basu et al.) are known to have complexity that is doubly exponential in the number of quantifier blocks and can be practically infeasible; since the practical motivation of the paper is hyperparameter tuning, the lack of any discussion connecting the statistical guarantee to an actual tractable (or even approximate) tuning algorithm is a substantial limitation that is not acknowledged.

The central technical contribution is largely a transplant/refinement of existing tools (Basu et al.'s quantifier elimination complexity theorem and the Goldberg-Jerrum/Bartlett et al. GJ-algorithm pseudo-dimension framework) rather than a fundamentally new proof technique; the main novelty is in bookkeeping the complexity parameters to extend from scalar to vector hyperparameters and from f≡g to f≠g, which, while useful, is a fairly incremental generalization once the FOL viewpoint is adopted.

The two 'new applications' (weighted group LASSO and weighted fused LASSO) are somewhat narrow and stylized; neither is contextualized with any realistic numerical scale, nor is there discussion of why these particular bounds (e.g., O(p^3 d + p^2 d^2)) are practically meaningful compared to naive covering-number or discretization arguments.

There are minor presentation/consistency issues (e.g., 'Forth' instead of 'Fourth' in the contributions list; Appendix F.2 refers to 'Theorem 7.1' when the relevant result is Theorem 7.2), suggesting the manuscript could benefit from another careful proofreading pass.

The related work discussion is relatively thin, focusing almost exclusively on direct comparison with Balcan et al. (2025) and Goldberg & Jerrum (1993); broader connections to other statistical/algorithmic approaches to multi-dimensional hyperparameter search (e.g., results with partial smoothness assumptions, or other relaxations of the piecewise-polynomial structure) are not discussed, making it harder to judge the work's positioning relative to the wider literature.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified open problem (generalization guarantees for multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning in data-driven algorithm design), directly extending Balcan et al. (2025) beyond scalar hyperparameters.

The core technical device—reducing pseudo-dimension bounds to the logical (quantifier-elimination) complexity of FOL-definable loss functions—is elegant, general, and cleanly separates the model-theoretic machinery (Theorem 4.1) from its applications (Theorems 5.1, 6.1, 7.2).

The framework removes the restrictive regularity assumptions (e.g., ELICQ conditions) required by prior geometric arguments, and extends naturally from the single-level (f ≡ g) setting to the practically important bilevel validation setting (f ≠ g), which better reflects real train/validation splits.

Theorem 4.1 is shown to strictly improve upon the previously best general bound (Goldberg & Jerrum, 1993), with a concrete and interpretable gain (removal of dependence on data dimension q and an extra factor of p).

Section 7's refined analysis via explicit solution paths is a nice practical sharpening, and the paper carefully demonstrates tightness for a nontrivial example (data-driven ElasticNet) by matching a known lower bound from Balcan et al. (2023), lending credibility to the overall approach.

The applications to weighted group LASSO and weighted fused LASSO are good demonstrations of the framework's reach beyond piecewise-polynomial structures (group LASSO) and showcase how additional structure (explicit solution path via mp-QP duality) yields tighter bounds (fused LASSO).
Proofs appear to be carried out carefully and in detail in the appendix, with explicit FOL constructions, complexity bookkeeping, and sketch-to-detail traceability.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical illustration (not even a toy numerical sanity check) of how the derived pseudo-dimension bounds compare to actual sample complexity needs or how loose/tight they are in practice, which would strengthen the practical significance claims.

Tightness of the main general-purpose bounds (Theorems 5.1 and 6.1) is left completely open; only the specialized Section 7 setting (explicit solution paths, e.g., ElasticNet) is shown to match a lower bound. It remains unclear how loose the general training/validation loss bounds are, which somewhat tempers the claimed resolution of the open question.

The polynomial-degree growth in p and d (e.g., p²d² or p³d terms) in the bounds could be quite large in realistic multi-dimensional tuning regimes, and the paper does not discuss how this compares to naive baselines (e.g., simple grid-search/VC bounds) to contextualize practical usefulness.

Assumption 3.2 (piecewise polynomial structure) and its ubiquity are asserted largely by citation rather than demonstrated rigorously for genuinely multi-dimensional/bilevel settings beyond the two LASSO examples provided; a wider range of applications (e.g., more complex ML pipelines, neural-network hyperparameters) would better substantiate the claimed generality.

The writing, while technically precise, is dense and defers most substantive content (including all full proofs and many structural complexity derivations) to the appendix, which may limit accessibility for readers less versed in real algebraic geometry/quantifier elimination.

Minor restrictive technical assumptions (e.g., full column rank of A in the weighted fused LASSO example, boxed/bounded domains for A and Θ) are used without much discussion of how binding or realistic these are, nor how the bounds would change in their absence.

The paper does not discuss computational aspects of actually performing ERM over the multi-dimensional hyperparameter space in practice (even approximately), so while learnability is established in a statistical sense, the algorithmic tractability of exploiting these guarantees is left unaddressed.

strengths: Addresses an explicitly stated open problem from prior work (Balcan et al. 2025): extending generalization guarantees for data-driven hyperparameter tuning from one-dimensional to multi-dimensional hyperparameters, and from the restrictive f≡g (training-loss only) setting to the more realistic f≠g (validation-loss) bilevel setting.

The core technical tool (Theorem 4.1) connecting pseudo-dimension to logical/quantifier-elimination complexity of polynomial FOL formulas is clean and demonstrably sharper than the prior Goldberg & Jerrum (1993) bound, removing an unnecessary dependence on the ambient data dimension q and a factor of p in front of log M.

The paper supplies both an upper bound (Theorem 5.1, 6.1) and, notably, the first lower bound (Theorem 5.2) for this general implicit bi-level setting, giving some sense of tightness; the bit-extraction/stabilization argument for coercive functions used in the lower bound is a non-trivial technical contribution.

Section 7 shows how additional structure (explicit rational solution paths) yields substantially tighter bounds that remove dependence on the inner-dimension d, and the authors verify this bound is tight by recovering the known matching lower bound for ElasticNet tuning from Balcan et al. (2023), which is a nice sanity check on the framework's utility.

The framework's applicability extends beyond the piecewise-polynomial assumption of the prior work to general semi-algebraic functions, demonstrated concretely with new learnability results for weighted group LASSO and weighted fused LASSO — problems that could not be handled by the earlier geometric approach.

The paper is reasonably well organized, with proofs deferred to appendices and the logical structure of the argument (FOL construction → quantifier elimination → GJ algorithm → pseudo-dimension bound) clearly laid out and reused consistently across sections.
weaknesses: The paper is entirely theoretical with no empirical illustration or numerical validation of the bounds (e.g., simulated experiments comparing empirical sample complexity to the derived Pdim bounds, or a demonstration that ERM over the induced function classes is tractable in practice). Even a small numerical sanity check would strengthen confidence that the bounds are not merely a formal exercise.

The magnitude/looseness of the bounds in practical regimes is not discussed; the polynomial dependencies on p, d, and quantifier-elimination blow-up (e.g., iterated products over quantifier blocks) could make bounds vacuous for even moderately sized problems, and the paper does not quantify this.

The lower bound (Theorem 5.2) is only established for the training-loss (f≡g) case; a general lower bound for the more important validation-loss (f≠g) bi-level setting is left open, which somewhat limits the completeness of the 'tightness' claim advertised in the abstract/contributions.

Computational tractability of the proposed approach (i.e., of actually performing empirical risk minimization or quantifier elimination in these settings) is not addressed; the framework establishes statistical learnability but says nothing about whether the resulting ERM problem is efficiently solvable, which is an important practical gap given the paper's motivation of 'automating hyperparameter tuning.'

The degree of technical novelty relative to Balcan et al. (2025) and the earlier Goldberg-Jerrum/Bartlett et al. GJ-algorithm machinery is somewhat incremental in spirit (applying known quantifier-elimination and GJ-algorithm machinery to a generalized multi-dimensional/bi-level setting), even though the specific derivations and the tightening of the earlier logic-based bound are non-trivial.

The presentation, while systematic, is extremely dense and notation-heavy, which may hinder accessibility; some intuition for why the quantifier-alternation structure K stays bounded/small across the applications (rather than growing with problem complexity) could be made more explicit earlier in the main text rather than only via examples.

The paper's discussion of related work on empirical hyperparameter-tuning methods (Bayesian optimization, Hyperband, etc.) in the introduction is somewhat superficial and mainly serves as a rhetorical contrast rather than a rigorous comparison of theoretical guarantees, slightly overstating the gap being filled.

strengths: Addresses an explicitly stated and practically important open problem (generalization guarantees for multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning), moving beyond the one-dimensional scalar setting of Balcan et al. (2025).

The core technical device—reducing the threshold indicator of an implicitly (bi-level) defined loss to a polynomial first-order logic (FOL) formula and then invoking quantifier elimination plus the Goldberg-Jerrum framework—is a clean and reasonably general way to sidestep ad hoc geometric arguments (e.g., ELICQ-type regularity conditions) required by prior work.

Theorem 4.1 improves on the classical Goldberg & Jerrum (1993) bound by removing dependence on the instance/data dimension q and a factor of p in front of log M, which is a concrete, verifiable technical improvement.

The paper supplies a lower bound (Theorem 5.2) for the training-loss setting using a non-trivial bit-extraction/stabilization argument adapted to the implicit (arg min) structure, which is new relative to prior data-driven tuning literature that lacked lower bounds in this general setting.

The framework is shown to extend beyond piecewise-polynomial structure to general semi-algebraic functions (Appendix C), and this is demonstrated concretely via the weighted group LASSO application (Section 8.1), broadening the scope of applicability.

The solution-path-based refinement (Section 7) is a nice complementary contribution, showing that when explicit rational solution paths exist, the quantifier-elimination machinery can be bypassed to get bounds independent of d, and the ElasticNet case (Appendix F.2) is shown to match the known lower bound from Balcan et al. (2023), giving some validation of tightness in a special case.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical illustration whatsoever—not even a toy numerical experiment to show how the derived (often very large, e.g., O(p^3 d + p^2 d^2) or O(p d^2 log M_tot + p^2 d^2 log Δ_tot)) bounds compare to actual sample complexity needed in practice, leaving the practical relevance of the main results largely unverified.

There is a clear mismatch between the general upper bound for the training-loss setting (Theorem 5.1: O(pd log(...) + p^2 d log Δf)) and the lower bound the paper itself proves (Theorem 5.2: Ω(pd log Δf)); the p^2 vs. p gap is not discussed or reconciled, undermining the claim that the bounds are broadly tight (tightness is only demonstrated in the special ElasticNet case under the stronger explicit-solution-path assumption of Section 7, not for the general framework of Sections 4-6).

The core proof technique is largely an assembly of pre-existing machinery (Basu et al.'s quantifier elimination complexity results, the Goldberg-Jerrum pseudo-dimension framework, and standard logical manipulations such as A⇒B ≡ ¬A∨B); while the application to this specific bi-level, multi-dimensional setting is new, the mathematical novelty beyond combining known tools is modest.

The structural assumptions (bounded box domains for A and Θ, piecewise-polynomial/semi-algebraic structure with instance-independent complexity parameters, the optimistic bi-level formulation) are nontrivial and their scope of applicability to realistic, high-dimensional ML pipelines (e.g., neural network hyperparameters, non-convex training losses) is not discussed in depth beyond citing that such structure is "ubiquitous."

The paper does not address the computational/algorithmic side of actually performing empirical risk minimization over the multi-dimensional hyperparameter space once the generalization bound is established; sample complexity control alone does not imply an efficient tuning procedure, and this gap between statistical guarantee and practical algorithm is not acknowledged as a limitation.

The presentation is extremely dense, pushing almost all substantive proofs to the appendix and leaving only proof sketches in the main text; combined with heavy FOL/model-theoretic notation, this significantly limits accessibility even for a theoretically-inclined ICML audience, and could be improved with more intuition-building examples or discussion of why the bounds have the specific exponents they do.

The two showcased applications (weighted group LASSO, weighted fused LASSO) are somewhat contrived demonstrations of framework generality rather than problems with independent practical motivation or evaluation; the resulting bounds (particularly for group LASSO) are high-order polynomials in p and d, raising doubts about whether these guarantees are ever non-vacuous for realistic sample sizes.

strengths: Resolves a clearly stated and well-motivated open problem: extending generalization guarantees for data-driven hyperparameter tuning from the one-dimensional case (Balcan et al. 2025) to the practically important multi-dimensional setting (\alpha \in R^p).

The core technical contribution (Theorem 4.1) is a clean and general bridge between logical definability (polynomial FOL) and pseudo-dimension via quantifier elimination, which is shown to strictly improve upon the only prior comparable bound (Goldberg & Jerrum 1993), removing an unnecessary dependence on data dimension q and a factor of p.

The framework removes the restrictive regularity assumptions (e.g., ELICQ conditions) required by the prior geometric approach, and naturally extends to the f \neq g (training vs. validation objective) bilevel setting, which is of clear practical relevance since training and validation sets should be distinct.

A first lower bound (Theorem 5.2) is established via a non-trivial bit-extraction/stabilization argument adapted to the implicit bilevel optimization setting, which substantiates the tightness of the upper bounds in at least some regimes.

Section 7's refinement using explicit solution paths yields tighter, dimension-independent (in \theta) bounds, and the authors show this refined bound exactly recovers a known matching lower bound for ElasticNet tuning (Balcan et al. 2023), providing concrete evidence of tightness.

The framework's scope is demonstrated to extend beyond piecewise polynomial functions to the broader semi-algebraic function class, illustrated via new learnability results for weighted group LASSO (not piecewise polynomial) and weighted fused LASSO (with an improved O(d^2) bound derived via the dual mp-QP solution path).
Proofs are detailed and appear carefully constructed, with appendices providing full technical arguments for all claimed theorems.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation; there is no numerical illustration of how the derived bounds behave in practice, how loose/tight they are for realistic problem sizes, or whether ERM is computationally tractable for the considered examples.

The approach relies heavily on existing heavy machinery (Basu et al.'s quantifier elimination algorithm and the Goldberg-Jerrum/Bartlett et al. GJ framework); while the combination and application to the multi-dimensional bilevel setting is new and non-trivial, the core proof technique is largely an adaptation of known tools rather than a fundamentally new mathematical technique.

Computational tractability of actually performing the quantifier elimination / ERM implied by the framework is not discussed; for problems with many quantifier alternations K, the complexity bounds in Theorem 2.5 can blow up badly (towers of exponentials in general), and the paper does not discuss how this affects the practical usability of the framework beyond the statistical learning guarantee.

The lower bound (Theorem 5.2) is only established for the training-loss (f \equiv g) setting; no lower bound is given for the general validation-loss (bi-level, f \neq g) setting, which the authors themselves acknowledge as an open question, leaving a gap in understanding the tightness of Theorem 6.1.

Some structural assumptions (e.g., boxed hyperparameter/parameter domains, non-emptiness of S(x,\alpha) for all (x,\alpha), uniform bounds M, \Delta across all problem instances) are somewhat strong and their verification in new applications may require nontrivial additional analysis (as shown by the lengthy derivations needed for the two example applications in Section 8).
